guide.summary: Selected Works (40% of the score) presents 5 works that demonstrate your strongest skill and the purposeful use of materials, processes, and ideas, each identified with brief written information.

sections.heading: Choosing works
sections.body: Choose five works that show the highest level of drawing skill and the clearest connection among materials, processes, and ideas. They may come from your Sustained Investigation or elsewhere, and they don't need to share a theme. Variety can show range, but each piece must be strong on its own. Avoid works that depend on explanation to succeed visually.

sections.heading: Skill
sections.body: Readers look for control and intention in drawing skills: mark-making, line quality, surface manipulation, the illusion of depth and space, light and shade, and composition, using elements and principles of art and design. Every visual choice should support the composition and idea. Purposeful decision-making matters more than polish, but weak craft can undermine strong ideas.

sections.heading: Identifying information
sections.body: For each work, you state the ideas, materials, and processes in a few words. Be precise: name actual materials and techniques, and state the idea concisely. Example: 'Ideas: fading memory of a family kitchen. Materials: vine charcoal, kneaded eraser, toned paper. Processes: layering, smudging, subtractive erasure.' Accurate identification helps readers see the relationship between your choices and your intent.

sections.heading: Evaluating your own work
sections.body: Before selecting five works, evaluate each piece honestly. Ask whether the composition is intentional, whether line quality, value, texture, space, light and shade, and composition support the idea, and whether the craft is controlled. Look at the work from a distance and in a photograph, since readers see only images. Ask peers what they notice first and what they think the work is about; if their answers differ from your intent, the work may need revision or may not be your strongest choice. Choose works that hold up visually without explanation.

sections.heading: Showing range and strength
sections.body: Selected Works can come from your Sustained Investigation or other projects. A strong set might include different materials or approaches within drawing, but every piece must be strong. Readers value works where mark-making, hatching, blending, erasure, and surface manipulation clearly serve the idea. A smaller range of excellent works is better than a wide range with weak pieces. Make sure each work's identifying information names specific ideas, materials, and processes.

sections.heading: Photographing for scoring
sections.body: Photograph each work in even, indirect light, with the camera parallel to the surface to avoid distortion. Crop out backgrounds, correct color to match the original, and save at the required resolution. For works with texture or fine detail, consider a separate detail image in the Sustained Investigation. A poor photograph can lower the perceived quality of excellent work.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body: Students sometimes choose works for sentimental reasons, include pieces with unresolved areas, or write vague identification. Ask a teacher to review your selection, revise weak areas when possible, and check that every identification line is precise and accurate.

sections.heading: What readers look for
sections.body: Readers evaluate Selected Works on skill and on the relationship among materials, processes, and ideas. In drawing, skill means purposeful control: compositions that guide the eye, deliberate use of elements and principles, and confident handling of materials. The relationship among materials, processes, and ideas means your choices make sense for what you are trying to communicate. A technically impressive work with no clear idea, or an interesting idea with weak execution, scores lower than a work where both are strong and connected.

sections.heading: Worked example: choosing between two works
sections.body: Suppose you must choose between a highly detailed realistic piece made early in the year and a more experimental piece made later. Ask which shows stronger decision-making and a clearer connection between technique and idea. If the experimental piece communicates its idea more powerfully and shows confident handling of materials, it may be the better choice even if it looks less polished. Readers value intentional, sophisticated work over sheer detail.

sections.heading: Writing identification lines
sections.body: Each Selected Work needs brief identification of ideas, materials, and processes. State the idea in a phrase, list the actual materials, and name the key processes. Avoid vague terms like 'mixed media' without specifics or 'emotions' without saying which ones. Precise identification helps readers understand your intent quickly.

keyTakeaways: Works may come from the SI.
commonMistakes: Choosing favorite works instead of strongest works.
Works that need explanation to succeed.
examTips: Ask a teacher or peers to rank your works.

practice.prompt: Describe how you will choose your 5 Selected Works from 12 finished pieces.

rubric.description: Connects criteria to the rubric (skill; materials, processes, ideas).

practice.sampleResponse: I'll rate all 12 works on skill, on how clearly materials and processes serve the idea, and on whether each succeeds without explanation. My teacher and two classmates will rank their top five independently, and I'll compare. I'll drop any work with a weak area of craft and keep variety only if each piece is strong.

practice.prompt: Write identification lines (ideas, materials, processes, a few words each) for one of your works, then explain in 2–3 sentences why your choices fit the idea.
practice.sampleResponse:
Ideas: fading memory of a family kitchen. Materials: vine charcoal, kneaded eraser, toned paper. Processes: layering, smudging, subtractive erasure.
Why: These materials allow layering and removal, so the surface literally shows what is added and lost. The process mirrors how memory builds up and fades.

practice.prompt: Analyze a work of your own (or an imagined one): explain how it demonstrates drawing skills, naming at least two specific elements or principles and their effect.
practice.sampleResponse: A diagonal of repeated shapes leads the eye from the lower left to the figure, creating movement. High contrast between the dark background and the light figure creates emphasis, so the viewer reads the figure first. Empty space on the right suggests the absence the work is about.

practice.prompt: Identify the weakest of your five Selected Works and propose a specific revision or replacement plan.

rubric.description: Explains how changes strengthen skill or synthesis.

practice.sampleResponse: My weakest work has a muddy middle-value range, so the forms flatten. I'll deepen the darkest values and lift the highlights to widen the range, then rephotograph it. If it still lacks a focal point after two weeks, I'll replace it with a stronger piece from my investigation.
